source.title: Generative modeling of intrinsically disordered protein regions by reinforcing sparse autoencoder features
source.authors: J. Liu; Sebastian Ibarraran; Frank Hu; Soojung Yang; Xin-Yu A. Feng; A. Park; A. Aneesh; Lacramioara Bintu; Alexander R. Dunn; Grant M. Rotskoff

record.file_problem: none; the full paper text, including appendices, is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study trains an SAE on a protein language model and reports that enriched SAE features correspond to recognizable sequence grammars, extending evidence about SAE-recoverable features to a protein-model setting. It does not test superposition geometry or the other claim versions.
record.gate_note: The paper also reports results from RL-SAE and activation steering, but those intentionally induce targeted feature activations; they are not evidence that features arise or are represented that way without inducement. Those intervention results are therefore not rows for the claim. Feature-enrichment values used to select features are not recorded as results; the reported qualitative feature-to-grammar findings are.
record.test_reason: The paper trains a Top-k SAE on a protein language model and reports that enriched features match known sequence grammars. That is a result on SAE-recoverable features in a new setting, which bears on V4. It does not test the toy-model, capacity, polysemanticity, canonicality or dimensionality versions.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is broadly right. The authors say enriched SAE features recover canonical IDR sequence grammars, which makes them interpretable design targets for RL-SAE. They draw no conclusions about superposition.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses an SAE trained on protein-language-model activations and evaluates enriched sequence features; it does not use the toy-network superposition method or test overlapping, near-orthogonal feature directions.
record.method_sensitivity: The SAE characterization reported here uses IDR-position activations from layer 18 of the 24-layer IDiom-300M model; the paper does not report a comparison of feature-grammar results across layers or model sizes.
record.problems: The evidence relevant to V4 is qualitative and shown for four example sequence sets; the reported feature-to-grammar correspondence is not a test of superposition or feature geometry. The paper's evaluations are computational, and the authors state that experimental validation is needed for biological function.
record.rows_left_out: No additional non-induced results directly bearing on a listed claim version were identified. Intervention results from RL-SAE and activation steering were omitted because the target feature activations are induced by design.

untested.parts: Toy-model geometry, the sparsity transition, and near-orthogonality are not tested.
Capacity competition and importance-based allocation of dimensions are not tested.
Non-capacity causes of polysemanticity are not tested.
Spreading of features across neurons and evidence from natural-language LLMs are not tested. No reconstruction-sparsity tradeoff is analysed beyond the layer sweep in Figure 7.
Completeness, stability and canonicality of SAE features are not tested. Random-feature and top-feature RL results use SAE features only as design targets.
One-dimensional versus multi-dimensional features are not tested.

missing.what: Appendix R logo galleries for all eight sets show the top-30 features. Some, such as the P-body RG/RGG motif, are noted as only weakly present. This qualifies the claim that enriched features recover grammars.
missing.locator: §5.2.3 text on P-body motif; Appendix R, Figures 13-20

record.verdict_notes: The RL-SAE and steering results are induced by design and were correctly excluded. Evidence for V4 is weak and qualitative, and the paper only incidentally relates to superposition. The random-feature control in Appendix K shows that RL-SAE on random features can reach high feature-firing coverage but does not raise ProtGPS scores. This bears on how meaningful enriched features are, not on V4 directly.

versions.untested_parts: Toy-model superposition, overlap geometry, sparsity-dependent transitions, and regular geometry are not tested.
The study does not test whether polysemanticity results from competition for limited representational capacity or whether feature importance determines dedicated versus shared dimensions.
The study does not investigate alternative causes of polysemantic neurons or whether polysemanticity is evidence for superposition.
Tests SAE-recoverable sequence features in a protein language model, not feature spreading across neurons or evidence across other LLMs.
The study uses SAE features as design targets but does not test whether they are complete, stable, or canonical units of the model's representation.
The study does not compare one-dimensional feature directions with multidimensional features or test superposition geometry.

rows.measure: Whether enriched SAE features correspond to recognizable biological sequence grammars
rows.value: Top enriched features correspond to the canonical FG/GLFG repeat grammar in NPC sequences.
rows.note: The text describes the top-four enriched features; this is qualitative evidence of recognizable SAE-associated patterns, not a test of superposition geometry.
rows.check: The correspondence is qualitative, from the top-four features shown in Figure 2. It is not a measured rate, and the baseline is not stated. The row is acceptable as a weak V4 row. V4 names feature spreading across neurons or SAE-recoverable sparse features, and this is only the SAE-recoverable part.

relationships.condition: IDiom-300M protein language model, layer-18 Top-k SAE, four example sequence sets (NPC, speckle, activation domains, repression domains)
relationships.reason: Top enriched SAE features match known grammars such as FG/GLFG repeats and RS repeats in all four shown sets (r1-r4). This is qualitative and limited to the examples shown.
relationships.display_finding: The top enriched SAE features matched known grammars such as FG/GLFG and RS repeats in all four sequence sets shown, though this is qualitative and limited to those examples.
